opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's real progress, and I want to give credit where it's due. Some of these services now run in a handful of cities with no safety driver, and that is genuinely impressive engineering. A decade ago a lot of people said it couldn't be done at all, and it's being done, at least in some places.

But I'd put a big asterisk on it, and the asterisk is about generalization. These systems work best in carefully mapped areas, often with good weather, with remote human operators who can step in when the car gets confused, and with years of data collection on those particular streets. That's not the same as what people were promised around 2016, which was that you'd buy a car, it would drive itself anywhere, and we'd have millions of them on the road by 2020. That didn't happen, and the reason it didn't happen is exactly the thing I've been banging on about for years: the long tail of outliers.

Driving is mostly routine, but every so often you hit something the system hasn't seen. A strange construction configuration, a police officer waving you through a red light, a person in a costume, a fire hose across the road. Humans handle those cases with common sense and a model of how the world works. Systems that are largely built on pattern recognition over huge amounts of data handle them much less gracefully, because the novel case is by definition not well represented in the training data. You see that in the incidents: cars getting stuck, blocking emergency vehicles, doing odd things around unusual scenes. Each one gets patched, but patching edge cases one at a time is not the same as having a system that actually understands what it's doing.

So my assessment is: impressive, narrow, expensive, and slow to scale. It's a good lesson for AI more broadly. People look at large language models now and say, "We're almost there, just a little more data." Driverless cars are the cautionary tale. Getting to ninety-nine percent can happen fairly quickly; getting the last fraction of a percent, the part that really matters for safety and trust, can take decades, and it may require different ideas, more structured world models, more reasoning, maybe hybrid neurosymbolic approaches, rather than just scaling up what we already have.

r001.rationale: It says some services run without a safety driver, while remote human operators can still step in when cars get confused.

r002.rationale: It notes services operate in only a handful of cities and describes them as narrow, but does not say they remain demonstrations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's genuinely impressive and genuinely limited at the same time, and people tend to want to pick one of those. You can get in a Waymo in Phoenix or San Francisco and it will take you across town without a driver, and ten years ago that would have seemed like science fiction. I don't want to take that away from them. I've ridden in them. It's real.

But let's be honest about what it took to get there and what it tells us. It's been well over a decade, enormous amounts of money, something like a hundred billion dollars across the industry, and we have a handful of geofenced cities, heavy reliance on detailed maps, and remote operators standing by when the car gets confused. That's not what we were promised. In 2016 everybody was saying this would be a solved problem by 2020. Elon Musk said it every year. What we got instead is a very narrow, very expensive, very carefully constrained deployment.

And the reason it took so long is exactly the thing I've been saying about deep learning for twenty-five years. These systems are terrific at the cases they've seen and brittle at the ones they haven't. The long tail is the whole ballgame in driving. A plane that lands at a weird angle on the freeway, a person in a chicken suit directing traffic, a construction zone that doesn't look like the other construction zones. You can't memorize your way through an open-ended world. You need something like a model of what's going on, something like common sense, and the industry basically substituted brute force data collection and a lot of hand-engineered guardrails for that.

So my assessment is: Waymo has shown that if you throw enough engineering and enough constraints at a problem, you can get a system that works pretty well in a bounded environment. That's a real engineering achievement. What it has not shown is that we've cracked general intelligence, or even general driving. Cruise collapsed. Tesla's Full Self-Driving is still not full self-driving. And I'd say the gap between a demo in San Francisco and a car you can drop anywhere in the world, in any weather, with no map, is still exactly the gap between pattern matching and understanding. We haven't closed it. We've gotten better at hiding it.

r001.rationale: The response says the cars operate without a driver while remote operators stand by when they get confused, distinguishing the lack of an onboard driver from human operational support.

r002.rationale: The response notes that services are limited to a handful of geofenced cities, but describes Waymo’s bounded deployment as a real engineering achievement. It does not clearly judge current services to remain demonstrations because of that geographic limit.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s real progress, but we have to be careful about what we infer from it. You can now take a driverless taxi in some places, and that’s a substantial engineering achievement. But operating in a carefully delimited environment is different from being able to drive anywhere, under any conditions.

The hard question is what happens when something unusual occurs—a road layout the system hasn’t encountered, an unexpected maneuver, or a situation where a human would use common sense to work out what somebody else intends. Driving requires more than recognizing objects; it requires reasoning about how the world might change.

So I wouldn’t dismiss these services. But I also wouldn’t take their existence as evidence that we’ve solved general intelligence, or even all of autonomous driving. We should assess them by their reliability, the conditions under which they operate, and how they handle situations outside those conditions.

r001.rationale: It describes driverless taxis and their operating limits, but does not say whether humans provide operational support.

r002.rationale: It notes that services operate in carefully delimited environments and only in some places, but does not characterize them as demonstrations because of limited geographic availability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s real progress, but we need to be precise about what it demonstrates. Getting a car to drive without a human at the wheel in a bounded operating area is a substantial engineering achievement. It doesn’t follow that we’ve solved driving in general.

The hard question is how these systems cope with circumstances that differ from what they’ve encountered before: an unusual construction site, an ambiguous gesture from a pedestrian, some unexpected combination of events. Driving requires dealing with a very long tail of situations, and being very good at the common cases isn’t sufficient.

So I’d distinguish a useful service under particular conditions from a generally reliable autonomous driver. We should recognize the achievement while asking how much intervention and infrastructure it requires, how safety is measured, and whether that reliability carries over to new environments.

r001.rationale: It mentions driving without a human at the wheel and asks how much intervention is required, but does not clearly distinguish the absence of an onboard driver from human operational support.

r002.rationale: It notes operation in a bounded area and under particular conditions, but calls this a useful service and substantial achievement rather than judging the services to remain demonstrations because of limited geographic availability.
